title: Simple Doenjang Soup
subtitle: Everyday fermented soybean paste soup with tofu
excerpt: This is a quick everyday version of doenjang soup, not the longer-cooking doenjang jjigae. Anchovy stock is made in 10 minutes, doenjang is dissolved into it, and cubed tofu and courgette go in for a final 5 minutes. The whole thing is on the table in under 20 minutes. It serves 2 and is one of the most common soups eaten at Korean breakfast and dinner.
sourceNotes: Doenjang soup in some form has been eaten in Korea for over 2,000 years. Fermented soybean paste was one of the primary ways Koreans preserved protein and flavour before refrigeration, and diluting it into a broth with seasonal vegetables has been a daily practice across every region. This simpler version skips the long simmering of the jjigae tradition in favour of a clean, quick everyday soup.

glossaryTerms.definition: Doenjang is a Korean fermented soybean paste made from cooked soybeans that have been shaped into blocks, dried, and left to ferment with salt over months or years. It has a deep, earthy, pungent flavour that is saltier and more complex than Japanese miso. Doenjang is the base flavour of Korea's most important soups and stews. It is available in Korean supermarkets in tubs or pouches.

Anchovy stock, known as myeolchi yuksu, is the most common base stock in Korean cooking. It is made by simmering dried anchovies in water for 10 to 15 minutes, then removing the anchovies and using the resulting clean, subtly savoury liquid as the foundation for soups and stews. The stock is quick to make and adds a depth of flavour that plain water cannot replicate in Korean dishes.

content.text: This recipe serves 2 and takes under 20 minutes. This is a simpler, faster version than the slower-cooked doenjang jjigae: it uses the same
paste but relies on a quick
rather than a long simmer to develop flavour. It is the version most Korean households make on an ordinary weekday morning or evening.

Never boil the soup hard after adding the doenjang. High heat makes the paste taste raw and sharp rather than mellow and rounded. Once the doenjang is dissolved into the stock, keep everything at a gentle simmer until the vegetables are just cooked.
Make the anchovy stock. Place the dried anchovies in a medium saucepan with the water. Bring to the boil and simmer for 10 minutes. Remove and discard the anchovies.
Reduce the heat to a gentle simmer. Add the garlic and the doenjang paste. Stir until the paste is fully dissolved into the stock.
Add the courgette and simmer for 3 minutes.
Add the tofu cubes and continue to simmer gently for 2 minutes. Do not stir too vigorously or the tofu will break apart.
Add the spring onions in the final 30 seconds. Taste the soup. Doenjang is already quite salty, so add extra salt only if needed. Ladle into bowls and serve alongside rice.

items.symptom: Soup tastes raw and sharp rather than mellow
items.cause: The doenjang was added when the stock was boiling hard rather than at a simmer
items.fix: Reduce the heat before dissolving the doenjang. The paste needs a gentle simmer to mellow out its raw edge. If the soup tastes sharp, simmer on very low heat for an extra 5 minutes without boiling.

items.symptom: Tofu has broken into small crumbles throughout the soup
items.cause: The tofu was stirred too vigorously after being added
items.fix: Once the tofu is in the pot, stir only gently and minimally. A gentle swirl of the pot is better than using a spoon. Use firm tofu rather than silken, which breaks apart much more easily.

items.symptom: Soup is too salty to eat comfortably
items.cause: Too much doenjang was used or a particularly salty brand was used
items.fix: Add more water gradually, a splash at a time, tasting between each addition. Doenjang varies considerably in saltiness between brands. Start with 1.5 tablespoons next time and adjust to taste.

content.text: Doenjang soup is on the Korean table more often than almost any other dish. It is the soup of weekday mornings when there is no time for anything elaborate, and it is the soup that appears alongside dinner rice when something warm and uncomplicated is needed. The smell of doenjang dissolving into hot stock is one of the most recognisable kitchen smells in Korea. This simple version is the one made every day, not just on special occasions.
